content: India has experienced a significant reduction in the estimated number of HIV infections. In 2005, reports suggested that between 5.2 million and 5.7 million individuals were living with HIV. However, by 2007, UNAIDS estimated this number to have decreased to between 2 million and 3 million. This reduction places India's HIV prevalence rate at 0.36%, which is lower than that of several Western nations, including the United States, Canada, Italy, France, and Spain. The HIV epidemic in India is not uniform but consists of multiple localized epidemics, some of which coexist within the same state. The modes of transmission vary across regions. In many states, heterosexual transmission accounts for approximately 85% of cases, often linked to interactions with commercial sex workers. In contrast, in certain other states, intravenous drug use is the predominant route of HIV transmission. These regional variations make it particularly challenging for authorities and communities to monitor the epidemic and implement effective intervention programs. HIV surveillance in India is managed by the National AIDS Control Organization (NACO). Most of the surveillance data is collected through annual unlinked anonymous testing of individuals attending antenatal clinics (prenatal clinics) and sexually transmitted infection (STI) clinics. NACO publishes annual reports on HIV surveillance, which are accessible to the public on its official website. India faces unique challenges in addressing the HIV/AIDS epidemic due to its large population, high population density, low literacy rates, and consequently low levels of awareness about the disease. HIV/AIDS remains one of the most significant public health challenges the country has ever encountered. A study published in 2006 in the British medical journal The Lancet reported a roughly 30% decline in HIV infections among young women aged 15 to 24 years who attended prenatal clinics in selected southern states of India between 2000 and 2004. These southern states are considered to be areas where the epidemic is concentrated. The authors of the study cautiously attributed this decline to increased condom use among men who engage with commercial sex workers. They also cited several pieces of corroborating evidence to support this conclusion.
